bartok-bela-boulevard.description: A long Buda road climbing gently from the Gellért area through Móricz Zsigmond körtér towards the Feneketlen-tó lake, now lined with cafés, galleries and bookshops. It has carried several names since the 1870s and has been called Bartók Béla út since 1945.
paragraphs: Bartók Béla út is a main road in Budapest's 11th district, Újbuda. According to the Hungarian Wikipedia article on the street, it runs for about 2.96 kilometres between Szent Gellért tér and Vasút utca, crossing Móricz Zsigmond körtér and Kosztolányi Dezső tér on the way. It is one of the busiest radial roads of southern Buda. For visitors the interesting stretch is the one that rises gently from the Hotel Gellért area towards the Feneketlen-tó, the Bottomless Lake.

The street was not always named after the composer. The first section, from Szent Gellért tér to Móricz Zsigmond körtér, was called Fehérvári út from 1874 to 1920, and the outer section towards Kelenföld railway station was Átlós út from 1890 to 1920. In 1920 both were renamed Horthy Miklós út. The name Bartók Béla út dates from 1945. Building along the road followed the 1913 zoning plan, and it is lined mostly with residential blocks of three to five storeys.

Transport shaped the street early. A tram first ran along it in 1898, linking Kelenföld railway station with Móricz Zsigmond körtér, and in 1899 the Dél-Budai HÉV suburban railway began running from Szent Gellért tér along Fehérvári út. The tram depot at Kelenföld has operated since 1912. The same article notes that cobblestones were replaced with asphalt in 2002 and 2003, and that the tram track between Szent Gellért tér and Móricz Zsigmond körtér was renovated in 2016.

In recent years the road has been described as a success story. A We Love Budapest walk published in January 2022 calls it once neglected but now full of cafés, restaurants, galleries and boutiques. It mentions the Hadik café, an old literary café where Frigyes Karinthy, Dezső Kosztolányi and Tibor Déry met, and Pagony, described as Hungary's largest children's bookstore. It also lists small galleries including Godot Gallery, Zsófi Faur Gallery, Artphoto Gallery and Dokubrom, which shows archive photographs edited by the Fortepan team.

The walk in that article ends at the Feneketlen-tó, where it lists the Figaró Magic Shop, run by the Szabó family since 1969. By the lake's playground it also notes a statue of a teddy bear, Mackó, by the sculptor László Molnár, there since 1961. The Hungarian Wikipedia article adds that a programme called Bartók-negyed, started after the M4 metro opened and bus traffic fell, strengthened the cultural role of the stretch between Móricz Zsigmond körtér and Szent Gellért tér.
tips: Szent Gellért tér at the Danube end is the natural starting point; the We Love Budapest walk begins at Fővám tér on the Pest side and crosses Liberty Bridge.
The Feneketlen-tó park at the far end of the walk has tennis courts, a running track and an outdoor gym.
Cafés, shops and galleries change often, so check each venue's own page for current opening times before planning a stop.
Trams run along the street; check the BKK journey planner for current routes and service.

castle-garden-bazaar.description: A neo-Renaissance complex of arcades, stairways and gardens by Miklós Ybl at the foot of Castle Hill, beside the Danube. Built in the 1870s and 1880s, it later served as a rock-concert venue, then as a ruin, before its restoration and reopening in 2014.
paragraphs: The Castle Garden Bazaar, Várkert Bazár in Hungarian, is a neo-Renaissance complex of arcades, staircases and gardens on the Danube side of Castle Hill, at Ybl Miklós tér. It was built between 1875 and 1883 to plans by Miklós Ybl. According to the building's own history page, the idea arose in the early 1870s of a representative building complex and ornamental garden at the foot of the hill. Hungarian Wikipedia describes it as a listed monument and part of the Budapest World Heritage site.

A history of Buda Castle describes Ybl's design as an open arcade with pavilions, stairways, ramps and two blocks of flats. The arcades were meant to hold shops, stores and workshops, and the neo-Renaissance gardens were laid out to keep an open view of the Danube from the Royal Palace above. The sculptor Alajos Stróbl got the first studio in the arcade, in 1884, and about eighty other artists followed over the next century.

In the second half of the twentieth century the bazaar found a different life as the Budai Ifjúsági Park, the Buda Youth Park, which hosted pop and rock concerts from 1961 to 1984. Visit Hungary names bands such as LGT, Edda, Piramis, P. Mobil, Omega and Beatrice, and says inscriptions by Edda and LGT on a stone wall survived the later restoration. A P. Mobil concert on 23 September 1984 is described as the end of the Youth Park. The building was closed that year and decayed, and it was listed among the hundred most endangered monuments in the world.

A government decree of 2011 launched its reconstruction. According to Hungarian Wikipedia, the first phase reopened on 3 April 2014, and the second, with an event centre, underground garage and Renaissance garden, followed on 29 August 2014. Excavations during the work found medieval and Ottoman-era objects, remains of cannon foundries that operated here from the sixteenth to the eighteenth centuries, and, according to the building's own history page, several hundred carved stone and cast-iron bullets, probably from the 1686 recapture of Buda. Restorers also found an old lock with its broken key still inside, which has since been shown in several exhibitions.

The gardens are the part most visitors walk through. The Visit Buda Castle page mentions a Triton Fountain, a rose garden and stretches of old castle walls, and describes the building by the Danube bank as a home for exhibitions and cultural events. Do not confuse the bazaar with the Várkert-kiosk, a separate Ybl building nearby; the Buda Castle history notes that only these two of his works there survive.
tips: The gardens lie at the foot of Castle Hill beside the Danube bank, so they combine easily with a visit to the Castle District above.
Check the official Várkert Bazár site for current exhibitions, events and visiting conditions, as the building hosts cultural programmes.

When the building reopened in 2014, the Budapest History Museum's exhibition Ostromok és hétköznapok showed archaeological finds from the excavations in the southern palaces; check the official site for what is currently on show.

clark-adam-square-and-the-0-km-stone.description: The roundabout at the Buda end of the Chain Bridge, named after the engineer Adam Clark and home to the limestone 0 km stone from which Hungary's main roads are numbered. The Buda Castle Funicular and the tunnel under Castle Hill start here.
paragraphs: Clark Ádám tér is the square at the Buda end of the Chain Bridge, below Castle Hill. Visit Buda Castle calls it a symbolic starting point: the limestone 0 km stone stands here, beside the lower station of the Buda Castle Funicular, and the kilometre numbering of several of Hungary's main roads is counted from it. Hungarian Wikipedia adds that it marks the start of the first-class main roads except routes 1 and 8, and that the square lies at the entrance of the Buda tunnel.

The square has had several names. In the 1860s it was also called Népszínház tér, after the Buda People's Theatre that stood there, and from the mid-1870s Lánchíd tér, Chain Bridge Square. In 1912 it was renamed after Adam Clark, the Scottish engineer who designed the Chain Bridge and the tunnel. Hungarian Wikipedia calls it Budapest's first uniform neo-Renaissance square.

War and rebuilding changed it. The Budai Takarékpénztár building, designed by Miklós Ybl, was hit by a bomb in the Second World War. Hungarian Wikipedia says it was demolished in 1949 while the roundabout was being built, whereas We Love Budapest says the damaged parts came down in 1948 and a remaining torso only in 1990; a hotel now stands on the site. The Lánchíd Palota is the only original building left standing on the square. The square and the area around the 0 km stone were renovated in July 2014.

The stone itself is a limestone sculpture about three metres tall, with a zero sign and the letters KM on its pedestal. English Wikipedia credits the present sculpture to Miklós Borsos and dates it to 1975. It was not the first monument on the spot: in 1932 a statue of the Virgin Mary by Körmendi, put up by the Hungária Automobil Club, was the first monument here. Sources differ on its fate: English Wikipedia says the Second World War destroyed it, while We Love Budapest says it survived the siege but was removed by the communist authorities. From 1953 until the present sculpture replaced it, a sculpture of a worker stood here.
tips: The square is the lower terminus of the Buda Castle Funicular; check the official funicular page for its current operating status and tickets.
From the stone you can walk onto the Chain Bridge or into the Castle Hill area; the Buda tunnel entrance is at the square.
The roundabout is busy with traffic, so use the marked crossings when approaching the stone and take photographs from the small park around it.

vienna-gate.description: A rebuilt gateway at the northern end of the Castle District, where several well-known streets meet. The present gate dates from 1936, marking 250 years since the recapture of Buda, and replaced older gates that stood here since the Middle Ages.
paragraphs: The Vienna Gate, Bécsi kapu in Hungarian, stands at the northeastern corner of Vienna Gate Square at the northern end of the Castle District. It is the gate that linked the Castle to the road to Vienna. Visit Buda Castle calls it one of the most atmospheric entrances to Buda Castle and notes that several well-known Castle District streets begin at the square. Nearby it lists the Hungarian National Archives, the Lutheran church of Buda Castle and a notable grapevine.

A gate has stood here since the Middle Ages, and the names show its past. In the Middle Ages it was the Porta Sabbati, or Szombat-kapu, the Saturday Gate, after the weekly markets held in front of it. In the Ottoman period it was called Beç kapusu, and it was later also known as the Zsidó-kapu, the Jewish Gate. The Castle District heritage site says the medieval layout is known only from Baroque and late Ottoman plans, which show a tower where the wall sections met, with the passage through its ground floor.

The gate was rebuilt several times. A new one was built in 1723 and remained in use until 1849; another followed in 1850. In the early nineteenth century one of its two side gates was removed, and before the 1896 millenary festival the whole gate was pulled down. The present gate was built in 1936 to mark the 250th anniversary of the recapture of Buda from the Ottomans, and it resembles the destroyed one.

Wikipedia names the architect as Jenő Kismarty-Lechner and says the sculptor Béla Ohmann made the inscriptions, ornaments and reliefs, including a running angel. Memorials to the 1686 recapture stand on both sides: an angel statue on the left and a tablet on the right. Wikipedia describes the gate as more symbolic than functional. Two parts of the Bastion Promenade are connected across its top, and automatic barriers at the gate help control traffic within the Castle.
tips: Walk through the gate to see the angel statue and the tablet commemorating the 1686 recapture on either side.
The Lutheran church of Buda Castle and the Hungarian National Archives are close by on the square.
Several of the best-known Castle District streets start at the square, so it works well as an entry point for a walk through the district.

matthias-fountain.description: A neo-Baroque bronze fountain group by Alajos Stróbl in the Buda Castle palace forecourt, showing King Matthias Corvinus on a hunt. It was inaugurated in 1904, damaged in the Second World War, and is sometimes nicknamed the Trevi Fountain of Budapest.
paragraphs: The Matthias Fountain, Mátyás kútja, is a monumental fountain group in the western forecourt of Buda Castle, set against the northern facade of the former Castle Church. Visit Buda Castle places it in the Hunyadi Courtyard of the palace and describes it as Alajos Stróbl's sculptural composition evoking the legend of the Renaissance ruler, with cascading water. English Wikipedia calls the style neo-Baroque and says it is sometimes called the Trevi Fountain of Budapest.

The scene is a hunting party led by King Matthias Corvinus. The king stands on the highest rock in hunting dress with a crossbow in his right hand and a huge dead stag at his feet. Below him a henchman blows a horn, the leader of the hunting group sits on a boulder with his back to the viewer, and three hounds complete the central group. The bronze figures stand on heaps of rocks, with water running down between the boulders. The central niche forms a triumphal arch bearing the king's personal coat of arms.

Two figures sit at the sides of the basin. On the right is Szép Ilonka, Helen the Fair, protecting her tame fawn from the hunters. She is the heroine of a nineteenth-century ballad by Mihály Vörösmarty. On the left is Galeotto Marzio, an Italian chronicler who lived at Matthias's court, with a sighthound at his feet and a falcon on his fist.

Stróbl began work in 1899 after King Franz Joseph approved the composition. According to Wikipedia, the stag was modelled on a large animal killed by poachers in 1896 in a forest where Stróbl had gone hunting, and Duke Pálffy sent the hounds that served as models. The henchman figure won a state gold medal in 1901. The fountain was inaugurated in 1904 in the king's presence, and Alajos Hauszmann, master builder of the palace reconstruction, is credited with erecting it.

The Second World War destroyed the middle dog, which Jenő Grantner later reconstructed. The more elaborate original balustrade and mansard roof were simplified after the war damage, and the fountain was restored in 2010.
tips: Look for the details at the basin: Szép Ilonka and her fawn on the right, Galeotto Marzio with his falcon on the left.
The fountain is part of the palace grounds; check the official Buda Castle pages for current access to the courtyards.
The Savoyai Terrace and the Hungarian National Gallery are also in the palace area, so the two sights combine easily.

savoyai-terrace.description: A broad terrace in front of the Hungarian National Gallery on the Danube side of Buda Castle, with views of the Parliament, Gellért Hill and the bridges. Its centrepiece is József Róna's equestrian statue of Prince Eugene of Savoy, installed in 1900.
paragraphs: The Savoyai Terrace lies in front of the Hungarian National Gallery on the Danube side of the Buda palace. Visit Buda Castle says it offers a stunning view of the Danube, the Parliament, Gellért Hill and the bridges of Budapest, and that it features an equestrian statue of Eugene of Savoy. Wikipedia lists the Hungarian National Gallery, founded in 1957, among the palace wings labelled A to D.

The terrace is named after Prince Eugene of Savoy, born in Paris on 18 October 1663 and died in Vienna on 21 April 1736. According to Hungary Today he served as deputy commander of the Christian forces that liberated Buda in 1686. On 11 September 1697 he defeated a numerically superior Ottoman army at the Battle of Zenta, which the same article says ended roughly 150 years of Ottoman rule in Hungary.

The statue is the work of the sculptor József Róna. One account says the city of Zenta ordered it to commemorate the victory of 1697 but could not pay for the bronze, so it waited in Róna's studio and then in front of the Art Gallery's main entrance. Prime Minister Kálmán Széll suggested that Emperor Franz Joseph buy it, and he did, judging by photographs. It was installed in 1900 in front of the main facade of the Royal Palace. That account describes its style as Viennese neo-Baroque, chosen to harmonise with the horseshoe-shaped Baroque staircase behind it.

The palace around the terrace changed greatly in the twentieth century. English Wikipedia says fighting in the siege of 1944 and 1945 reduced the palace to ruins. The Baroque staircase was demolished in the 1950s and not restored, but the statue survived the siege relatively intact and returned to its original place after restoration.
tips: Come for the view: the terrace looks across the Danube towards the Parliament, with Gellért Hill and several bridges in sight.
The Matthias Fountain and the Hungarian National Gallery are in the same palace area, so the three sights fit into one visit.
Check the official Buda Castle and Hungarian National Gallery pages for current access conditions and events on the terrace.

cave-church.description: A church built into natural and artificial caves on the side of Gellért Hill, linked to the Pauline order. Founded after Hungarian pilgrims visited Lourdes in the 1920s, it was walled up under communism and reopened as that era ended; thermal water keeps the interior mild.
paragraphs: The Cave Church is built into the southeastern side of Gellért Hill, partly in a natural cave and partly in man-made chambers. Visit Buda Castle describes it as set in natural and artificial cave cavities and links it to the Pauline order. Visitors enter an outer cave and then follow a tunnel-like corridor to the deeper man-made church, where Masses and prayers are held. Visit Hungary says hot springs through the hill keep the interior at about 20 degrees Celsius all year.

The church grew out of a pilgrimage. According to We Love Budapest and Visit Hungary, Hungarian pilgrims who visited Lourdes in the 1920s proposed building a cave chapel inspired by the grotto there. We Love Budapest says it was consecrated in 1926, with the main altar in the outer cave and benches on the rock terrace outside; Visit Hungary gives 1931 as the year the construction was completed, so the sources differ. A legend recorded by We Love Budapest tells of a hermit named Iván who healed the sick with the bubbling waters at the cave's entrance.

In 1934 the Pauline order returned to Hungary after about 150 years in exile, bringing sixteen monks from Poland, according to We Love Budapest. Volunteers enlarged the cave with controlled explosions, and a neo-Romanesque monastery was built on the Danube side of the hill. During the Second World War the Pauline fathers sheltered civilians and refugees, sometimes disguising them as monks.

Under communist rule the monastic orders were abolished, the monks were forced out, the entrance was walled up with concrete and the cross above it was torn down. Sources differ on the date: We Love Budapest says the wall dates to 1960, Visit Hungary says only the 1950s, and Wikipedia and Aleteia say the cave was sealed in 1951. The wall was demolished as communist rule ended (Wikipedia gives 1989, Visit Hungary the 1990s), and the Pauline order restored the church. A section of the wall still stands on the right side of the entrance as a reminder.

Inside, the features named by the two sources include a bronze altar with a Polish eagle, a green pyrogranite altar made by the Zsolnay manufactory, a statue of Our Lady of Lourdes, a statue of Saint Stephen at the entrance and a ceramic relief of Saint Gellért. A relic believed to be part of the tibia of Saint Paul the Hermit, the Pauline order's most important relic, is also kept here.
tips: This is an active place of worship where Masses and prayers are held, so be considerate of worshippers.
Check the official Pauline Cave Church page for current visiting arrangements and the times and languages of services.
Look at the right side of the entrance for the preserved section of the concrete wall from the communist era.
The church is set in the side of Gellért Hill, so it combines naturally with other sights on the hill.

trinity-square.description: The main square of the Castle District, where Matthias Church, the Fisherman's Bastion and the Baroque Holy Trinity Column meet. The column was inaugurated in 1713 after a plague epidemic, and the square took its open shape only after the Ottoman rule ended in 1686.
paragraphs: Trinity Square, Szentháromság tér, is called the most significant square of the Buda Castle District by the district's heritage site. It lies where Tárnok, Szentháromság and Országház streets meet Hess András tér. Visit Buda Castle says the square, the richly decorated Holy Trinity Column, Matthias Church and the Fisherman's Bastion together create a setting that invites photography and strolling.

It is not an old square. Until the end of the Ottoman occupation in 1686 a block of houses stood on the site. The Town Hall and the Nagyboldogasszony parish church, today's Matthias Church, were joined only by a narrow lane, with a row of houses directly in front of the church. After the houses were demolished, the church frontage became visible and the area between church and Town Hall was opened up. A spring-fed well with a statue of Pallas Athene, the town's defender, was completed in 1718.

The Holy Trinity Column is the square's centrepiece. The Council of Buda decided in 1694 to erect a column against the plague, the foundation stone was laid in 1700, and the first statue was finished in 1706. In 1709, during another epidemic, it was removed to the Újlak suburb. The present column was built between 1710 and 1713 and inaugurated on 11 June 1713. The sculptor was Fülöp Ungleich, and Antal Hörger made the reliefs and coats of arms.

A hexagonal obelisk carries statues of Saint Roch, Saint John, Saint Christopher, Saint Augustine, Saint Joseph and Saint Sebastian, with reliefs of King David praying in repentance, the horrors of the epidemic in the Castle and the column itself. The Holy Trinity group crowns the top. The original sculptures are now in the Kiscelli Museum in Óbuda, and replicas stand on the monument.

Around the end of the nineteenth century the parish church was converted into a coronation church, the Jesuit buildings were cleared, and the former Ministry of Finance rose on the north side, opening the square towards the Fisherman's Bastion. The heritage site notes that the square's present form differs greatly from its Baroque layout because of replanning and reconstruction after the Second World War.
tips: Matthias Church and the Fisherman's Bastion stand on or beside the square; check their official sites for visiting conditions and tickets.
Walk around the Holy Trinity Column to find the six saints and the three reliefs described above.
The square is the heart of the Castle District, so it is a convenient base for nearby sights such as the Hospital in the Rock and the Vienna Gate.

st-stephen-s-hall.description: A reconstructed ceremonial interior in the Buda Castle palace, designed by Alajos Hauszmann around 1900 and gutted in the Second World War. Rebuilt over decades from photographs and plans, with a large Zsolnay ceramic fireplace, it opened to visitors in 2021.
paragraphs: St. Stephen's Hall, Szent István-terem, is a reconstructed ceremonial interior in the Buda Castle palace. It is named after Saint Stephen, founder of the Hungarian state, and was one of the most important interiors of the palace during the Dual Monarchy. Budapest.com says it was part of the palace's expansion after the Compromise of 1867, with architect Alajos Hauszmann designing it as the showpiece of the state rooms.

According to We Love Budapest, the original room had a carved ceiling, a large ceramic fireplace with Zsolnay depictions of Árpád-dynasty kings and saints, gilded furnishings and large chandeliers. Vilmos Zsolnay made the ceramics, Endre Thék the carved furniture and interior, and the Neuschloss brothers the parquet inlay. Budapest.com gives the fireplace as about 4.5 metres high and 2.5 metres wide, made of more than 600 pieces, with a bust of Saint Stephen by Alajos Stróbl on the mantelpiece. The interior was shown at the 1900 Paris World's Fair, where it won a top prize, before being installed in the palace. Emperor Franz Joseph called it very beautiful on his visit.

The hall hosted royal audiences and working lunches and served as a card room during balls. In December 1916, the day before the coronation of Karl I, the chest holding the Holy Crown was opened in the hall before the crown was taken to Matthias Church; this was the last ceremonial use of the room.

The Second World War ended the hall's life. The palace was bombed and fire gutted the interior, and the southern connecting wing suffered the most damage in the siege of 1944 and 1945. The room then stood unrestored and was used as storage for decades. Reconstruction began only in the post-communist era and took a long time, using archive photographs, plans, old invoices, duplicate ceiling pieces from the Zsolnay Quarter in Pécs and a transcript found in a villa on Lendvay utca. It was carried out under the National Hauszmann Program.

The reconstructed hall opened to the public in 2021, and We Love Budapest says visits are by guided tour. The accompanying exhibition, The Miracle of Buda Castle, includes a ten-door installation by Sam Havadtoy based on The Admonitions, a Latin text attributed to a foreign cleric and dated to around the 1010s. The hall also displays a very large herm, a sculpted likeness of Saint Stephen.
tips: Visits are by guided tour, according to a 2021 report; check the official St. Stephen's Hall site for current tours, languages and tickets.
Look first at the Zsolnay ceramic fireplace and the portraits of Árpád-dynasty kings and saints around the walls.
The hall is in the Buda Castle palace area, where the Matthias Fountain and the Savoyai Terrace also lie.

museum-of-fine-arts.description: Hungary's principal art museum, housed since 1906 in a neoclassical building on Heroes' Square. Its collections range from Egyptian antiquities and Greek and Roman art to Old Master paintings by Raphael, El Greco and Goya, sculpture, drawings and prints, shown alongside temporary exhibitions.
paragraphs: The Museum of Fine Arts, Szépművészeti Múzeum, is described by Finestre sull'Arte as the largest art museum in Hungary. It stands on Heroes' Square facing the Műcsarnok exhibition hall, and its holdings are organised into departments including Egyptian antiquities, classical antiquities, Old Master paintings, sculpture, graphics and art after 1800. Figures vary by source, but the collection runs to well over a hundred thousand works.

The decision to found the museum was made in 1896, and the site chosen was the square in front of the Műcsarnok. Albert Schickedanz and Fülöp Herzog designed both buildings, and the museum's eclectic neoclassical building was built between 1900 and 1906. It opened on 1 December 1906 in the presence of Emperor Franz Joseph, and the public could enter from 5 December. Its origins lie in collections from noble Hungarian families such as the Esterházy, Pyrker, Ipolyi and Jankovich, which the state acquired in the late nineteenth century.

The Old Master paintings number about three thousand and include Raphael's Esterházy Madonna, Correggio's Madonna of the Milk and works by Titian, Giorgione, Tintoretto, Dürer, Rubens, El Greco, Velázquez and Goya. The Egyptian collection includes painted mummy sarcophagi, and the classical collection includes 135 marble works acquired from Paul Arndt in 1908. Drawings and prints are shown in rotating exhibitions. A Giorgione painting was stolen in 1983 and recovered in Greece in 1984.

The twentieth century left its mark. The building was bombed in the Second World War, and part of the collection was taken to Germany. Works recovered in 1946 and 1947 were often damaged, and We Love Budapest notes that works taken by the Red Army remain in Russian museums. In 1957 the Hungarian artworks moved to the new Hungarian National Gallery, and the two institutions were reunited in 2012.

The museum closed on 15 February 2015 for a renovation led by the Mányi Studio. Its main aim was to restore the Romanesque Hall, which had been a storeroom for decades. Check the official museum site for the current galleries and exhibitions rather than relying on older reports.
tips: Heroes' Square and the Műcsarnok are directly beside the museum, so they combine naturally in one visit.
Check the official museum site for current opening times, tickets and temporary exhibitions before you go.
The collection is large; choose two or three departments, such as the Old Masters or the Egyptian collection, rather than trying to see everything.
The Romanesque Hall was restored as part of the museum's renovation; check which galleries are currently on show.

hospital-in-the-rock.description: A wartime emergency hospital built in the cave system under Castle Hill, later a secret Cold War nuclear bunker and now a museum. It treated casualties in the 1944 to 1945 siege and the 1956 uprising, and its wards and equipment can be seen on a guided tour.
paragraphs: The Hospital in the Rock and Nuclear Bunker Museum is housed in a natural cave system under Castle Hill, about ten kilometres long according to the museum's history page, which Budapest residents have used since the Middle Ages. The museum is at Lovas út 4/c and is run by a public benefit foundation. The first room built in the caves was the Air Raid Alarm Control Centre, which controlled the sirens in the Castle district from 1937 to 1945.

The hospital itself was built between 1941 and 1943 using existing cave tunnels, with caverns becoming wards and passages becoming corridors. It was ordered by Károly Szendy, then Budapest mayor and minister of war, and operated under St. John's Hospital. It opened on 20 February 1944 with three wards and one operating theatre. During the siege of 1944 and 1945 all 94 beds were constantly occupied and patients also lay in the cave corridors. The hospital had its own generators and could take X-rays when hospitals on the surface could not.

The history page records that eight Jewish doctors were assigned there to labour service, that Dr. Kálmán Koppány helped prevent their deportation, and that two of them were betrayed in November 1944 and one was killed. The breakout from the Castle came on 11 February 1945, after which less serious patients left and the rest were transferred. The museum's history page gives July 1945 as the closing date, while another account says June 1945. Other accounts give very different figures for how many wounded were treated at the peak of the siege.

In the 1950s the hospital became a top-secret institution with the code LOSK 0101/1, declassified in 2002. When the 1956 revolution began it reopened to treat civilians and soldiers, with Dr. András Máthé as head surgeon, and it operated until December 1956. Between 1958 and 1962 it was converted into a nuclear bunker with a ventilation system with a gas filter, a water supply connected to the Danube and two Ganz diesel engines. The plan was for medical staff to enter first and open the hospital for other survivors after 72 hours.

A caretaker family looked after the site until 2004, and the Krétakör Theatre Company staged performances there from 2004 to 2006. Renovation began in 2007, and it has been continuously open as an exhibition since 11 March 2008. Wikipedia notes that it features waxwork recreations of treatments and siege-era scenes.
tips: Visits are by guided tour; check the official Hospital in the Rock site for current tours, languages, tickets and booking.
A visitor guide suggests the Buda Castle Funicular from Clark Ádám Square, or bus lines 16, 16A or 116 to Dísz tér; check current routes before travelling.
The museum is a short walk from Matthias Church and the Fisherman's Bastion.
Guest reviews on the museum's site describe the tour as moving; it presents wartime suffering and the 1956 uprising.
